title: Peregrine - model catalog curation + benchmark handoff
next_steps: Jamie to send tailored pilot pricing and SOW by 2027-09-01
Marcus to share benchmark template and compatibility matrix CSV
Customer to provide sample prompt set and PII policy doc by 2027-08-30
Schedule technical walkthrough of VPC onboarding week of 2027-09-06

Marcus Li - upload compatibility matrix and bench template link - due 2027-08-27
Lucas Meyer - share sample prompt set and expected QPS - due 2027-08-30
Nina Ortiz - confirm VPC/KMS constraints and firewall policy - due 2027-09-03
summary: Short demo focused on Redwood model catalog curation workflow, how benchmarks map to runtime compatibility, and planning a pilot. Customer cares about cost/latency tradeoffs, VPC/KMS, and deterministic rollouts. Agreed next steps for pricing, bench templates, and VPC onboarding.
transcript:
[00:00] Jamie Ortega: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — this is Jamie from Redwood Inference. We\'ve got Marcus on the line for the deep catalog walk, and Priya from product for any console questions. How\'s everyone doing?
[00:10] Sara Patel: Good thanks, hey. We wanted to see how you help pick open models and how to map benches to our infra.
[00:18] Marcus Li: Cool; we\'ll go through the catalog UI, the compatibility matrix export, and then the bench template we use to interpret latency/cost. I\'ll call out where runtime kernels and quant profiles matter.
[00:30] Evan Ross: Quick note — our timeline is tight, targeted pilot in Q4, so we need clear success criteria and a lightweight SOW.
[00:38] Jamie Ortega: Yep, understood. Lucas, can you remind us of your current stack? I saw notes about GPU clusters and a mix of cloud/on-prem.
[00:45] Lucas Meyer: Right now we run most training and inference on GCP GPUs, some self-hosted k8s at edge sites. We have a 200 QPS target for core NLU routes, target p50 latency under 120 ms. Cost per 1k tokens is something we want to reduce vs monthly cloud spend.
[01:05] Marcus Li: Great, that helps. When we demo the catalog you\'ll see filters for architecture, memory footprint, and verified runtime profiles (we call them \"fit tags\"). Those fit tags encode whether a model runs on Triton-optimized kernels, FP16/INT8 quant paths, and the expected token throughput.
[01:25] Nina Ortiz: On the private side: we have strict KMS/HSM requirements and audit logs — SOC2 is in place but we need to confirm key residency.
[01:34] Priya Raman: We support KMS integrations and audit log exports; in Private mode your KMS can be customer-managed. We\'ll show the Console page that controls that.
[01:42] Sara Patel: Can you show how you pick which open models to shortlist? We have a long list — Llama variants, Mistral-ish, and a couple of smaller tuned models.
[01:55] Marcus Li: Absolutely. Switching to the catalog — you can start from a workload profile: chat vs completion vs embedding. For Peregrine\'s NLU route, I\'d pick models with low memory and fast kernel paths. You can then run an automated shortlist that scores by accuracy proxies and throughput.
[02:15] [screen share noise] Marcus Li: (narration) Here is search, I apply filters: parameter count < 20B, quant-friendly, and CPU offload supported. The shortlist exports a compatibility matrix CSV — column for model, expected throughput on target GPU, kernel notes, and fallback variant.
[02:38] Lucas Meyer: That CSV — is it the same as the compatibility matrix you mentioned in the RFP? We need that to feed into our cost model.
[02:45] Marcus Li: Yes, it\'s the same. We include a bench-suggested config per model: batch size, kv cache warmup, and quant profile. The bench template includes sample prompts, expected sequence length, and measurement hooks for p50/p90 latency and token-per-second.
[03:05] Sara Patel: How often are those fit tags updated? Open model ecosystem changes fast.
[03:12] Marcus Li: We run continuous bench sweeps weekly on our hosted catalog and monthly for dedicated capacity drivers; we also annotate when kernel changes or new quant kernels roll out. Customers can flag models to rebench in a sprint.
[03:30] Evan Ross: We care a lot about deterministic rollouts. If we pin to a model version, how do you handle auto-fallbacks if capacity is constrained?
[03:40] Jamie Ortega: Good question. In the routing layer you can pin a route to a model version and define a fallback chain — e.g., degrade to a smaller quantized variant or route to dedicated capacity pool. You can also set a rollout policy: canary then global.
[03:58] Lucas Meyer: What\'s the latency hit if you fallback to a quantized variant?
[04:04] Marcus Li: Typically quantized INT8 nets a 1.3-2x token throughput improvement on Ampere-like GPUs, but you should measure quality. We include BLEU-style or model-specific evals in the bench to quantify degradation.
[04:22] Nina Ortiz: KMS again — is the key ever exposed to Redwood? Our security team won\'t accept that.
[04:29] Priya Raman: In Private deployments the KMS stays in your cloud account; we call KMS just-in-time and never store keys. For hosted, we offer a bring-your-own-key flow via HSM connectors. We\'ll share the security whitepaper.
[04:44] Sara Patel: Okay — show us an end-to-end example: choose a model from the catalog, run bench, then map to runtime config.
[04:52] Marcus Li: Walkthrough: pick model X (small Llama-variant), click \"bench add\", select your prompt set (I recommend a representative 200 prompt sample), set target seq 256, and the bench returns p50/p90, throughput, memory high-water mark, and token cost estimate under various batchings.
[05:12] [brief pause, typing sounds] Marcus Li: Here\'s a bench run from a similar customer — p50 95ms at 50 QPS on a T4-equivalent with INT8, cost estimate 0.6 of your current baseline.
[05:31] Lucas Meyer: Those numbers are promising. Do you have automated guidance for batching thresholds? Our engineers don\'t want to tune every variant manually.
[05:40] Marcus Li: That\'s where Redwood Optimize suggestions come in — it analyzes your historical latencies and recommends batch sizes, KV cache TTL, and cacheable prefixes. The Console exposes suggested toggles and simulates cost impact.
[05:55] Evan Ross: How does caching interact with personalized prompts? We have per-user history we append.
[06:02] Marcus Li: Prefix caching is safe for deterministic system prompts and shared prefixes; per-user context is usually stored in KV but we warn about privacy considerations. Optimize will show hit rate estimates given your distribution.
[06:18] Sara Patel: For the pilot, we need 3 success metrics: max p50 under 120ms at 100 QPS, reduc token cost by 30% vs current, and zero exposure of keys.
[06:28] Jamie Ortega: Noted — those are measurable. We\'ll propose a pilot SOW with those KPIs.
[06:33] Nina Ortiz: On onboarding — how long to stand up a private control plane? Our compliance team wants it in our VPC.
[06:40] Priya Raman: Typical private control plane plus runtime in your VPC is 3-6 weeks depending on network approvals and firewall rules. We\'ll need your networking bastion IPs and KMS role. We can parallelize bench work using our hosted runners to accelerate model scouting.
[06:58] Lucas Meyer: If we run hosted benches, are prompts or data kept? We can\'t share PII.
[07:04] Marcus Li: Hosted bench runners use ephemeral storage and we recommend redacting PII. For highest security, run benches in your private cluster; we can provide the bench harness repo and a measurement script.
[07:18] Sara Patel: Show me the compatibility matrix details again — what fields are included?
[07:24] Marcus Li: Fields: model_name, family, parameter_count_est, memory_est, runtime_fit_tags, recommended_quant, expected_throughput_on_target_gpu, fallback_variant, note_on_kernels, bench_sample_id.
[07:38] Evan Ross: The \"note_on_kernels\" — can you expand? I want to know if a model needs a special kernel or an experimental op.
[07:44] Marcus Li: Sure — we\'ll flag experimental kernels and approximate risk. For example, some attention variants require a custom CUDA kernel; we\'ll note if it\'s in prod or experimental and include a mitigation plan.
[07:59] Nina Ortiz: Are SSO and RBAC available in the Console? We need SCIM sync and least privilege.
[08:05] Priya Raman: Yes, SSO via SAML/OIDC, SCIM for user provisioning, and role templates for read-only, infra-admin, and billing. All events are exported to your SIEM via our audit log stream.
[08:18] [background voice] Sara Patel: (quiet) good.
[08:22] Marcus Li: Returning to bench interpretation — when you run a bench we give a cost delta vs baseline and a confidence score. The confidence score comes from variability observed across runs and kernel stability.
[08:35] Lucas Meyer: Could you demo the Console view where Optimize suggests mixing two variants? We were thinking we might route 80% to a fast quantized model and 20% to a higher-accuracy variant.
[08:46] Marcus Li: Yes — in the Route config you can create traffic splits. The Console simulates cost + expected accuracy by combining benched metrics. I\'ll show an example: 80/20 split projected to meet p50 < 120ms and keep accuracy loss under 4% on our eval set.
[09:05] Evan Ross: That\'s helpful. Does Redwood host evals or do we supply our corp evals?
[09:11] Marcus Li: Both. You can upload your eval set; we keep results private. We also provide public metric harnesses for initial screening.
[09:20] Sara Patel: For the pilot, we want to focus on two models and a fallback plan; can you recommend the shortlist size?
[09:26] Marcus Li: Start with 3-5 models; run the bench template, then narrow to 1-2 for a pilot. The compatibility matrix helps you eliminate those with kernel risk or memory issues.
[09:36] Jamie Ortega: Quick commercial note — for pilots we can offer a pilot credit bundle and a discounted dedicated slot if you commit to a short reserved capacity. We\'ll include options in the SOW.
[09:47] Lucas Meyer: How do you measure quality regressions? We track rollbacks pretty tightly.
[09:52] Priya Raman: We integrate eval alerts with your repo of prompt tests. If a rollout causes a regression on any guardrail, automatic rollback triggers, and we send traces and diffs.
[10:04] [10:04 - 20:00: abbreviated bench demo and Q&A (screen share), intermittent chatter]
[20:01] Marcus Li: Jumping back — a couple of gotchas: (1) models that use fused attention ops sometimes need a specific CUDA toolchain; (2) per-token cost estimates can vary if you change batching. We surface both in the matrix.
[20:20] Nina Ortiz: Toolchain compatibility is a blocker for us if we have locked nodes. Can you provide kernel builds?
[20:27] Marcus Li: We can provide prebuilt kernels for supported toolchains and instructions to build in air-gapped environments. We\'ll note build complexity in the matrix.
[20:40] Sara Patel: Any red flags for our QPS target?
[20:44] Marcus Li: At 100 QPS and p50 < 120ms you\'ll likely need a combination of dedicated slots or heavier batching depending on average sequence length. If your seq average is 256, resource needs climb.
[20:58] Lucas Meyer: What\'s the recommended dedicated pool size starting point?
[21:02] Marcus Li: Roughly calculate tokens per second and map to the throughput per GPU in the matrix. We usually start customers with 2-4 GPUs in a dedicated pool for these loads while we converge on batching and cache TTL.
[21:17] Evan Ross: From a procurement view, any required terms we should prepare for? Data residency and indemnity were big items.
[21:24] Jamie Ortega: We\'ll share our standard enterprise addendum — it covers data residency, indemnity, and SOC2 attestation. Specific legal changes can be handled in the contract stage.
[21:35] Sara Patel: Can you also include a sample fallback policy in the SOW? We prefer an explicit A/B with fallback to a second model before hitting degraded UX.
[21:44] Jamie Ortega: Yep, will include a recommended fallback policy and the route YAML we\'ll use to implement it.
[21:50] [short pause] Marcus Li: One more technical note: our bench harness reports memory high-water marks that are conservative; in many cases the runtime squeeze can save ~5-10% memory. We\'ll call out optimistic vs conservative numbers.
[22:05] Lucas Meyer: If we run the bench locally and then onboard, do you import those bench results?
[22:11] Marcus Li: Yes, you can upload bench results; Console will merge them into the compatibility matrix to influence route suggestions.
[22:20] Nina Ortiz: Networking checklist — what do you need from us?
[22:25] Priya Raman: For private: public egress to our control plane endpoint, a small set of ingress rules for upgrade agents, and KMS role with limited permissions. We\'ll provide a checklist after this call.
[22:36] Sara Patel: About cost — if we commit to a dedicated pool, do you offer credits for the benching work?
[22:43] Jamie Ortega: We can apply pilot credits and offset bench running costs as part of the pilot package. We\'ll include the options in the proposal.
[22:52] Evan Ross: Can the bench template capture per-customer prompts and golden outputs for regression tracking?
[22:58] Marcus Li: Yes — we store golden outputs and diff on every run. If a rollout changes outputs beyond your threshold we\'ll trigger alerting.
[23:10] [23:10 - 28:00: deeper technical dive on quant profiles & kernel mapping, occasional cross talk]
[28:01] Marcus Li: I\'m going to show a compatibility example where a Llama-variant had an experimental fused-attention kernel; we recommended a fallback and tagged it in the matrix as \"experimental-kernel: avoid for critical flows\".
[28:20] Lucas Meyer: Good to know. What about quantization toolchain — do you recommend post-training quant or PTQ vs QAT?
[28:28] Marcus Li: For most open models PTQ works well with little dev overhead. If you need aggressive quality preservation, QAT is better but requires retraining. We include recommended quant profiles in the matrix.
[28:42] Sara Patel: Any integrations for tracing to our observability stack?
[28:47] Priya Raman: Yes — trace hooks, token-level latency breakdowns, and you can forward logs to your ELK or Datadog. We\'ll show the tracing dashboard.
[29:00] Marcus Li: (demo) here\'s a route dashboard showing token cost and per-token latency heatmap, and a link to the bench run id that produced the numbers.
[29:16] Evan Ross: If a bench indicates quality issues, what\'s the fastest mitigation path?
[29:21] Marcus Li: Options: change quant profile, increase batch to reduce cost, or route a fraction of traffic to a higher-accuracy variant. For critical regressions we recommend immediate rollback.
[29:35] Sara Patel: For SLOs we want canaries with automatic rollback on eval failure. Is that supported?
[29:40] Priya Raman: Yes — canary deploys with guardrail checks and auto-rollbacks are part of the rollout policy config.
[29:48] [29:48 - 40:00: follow-up nitty gritty — compatibility edge cases, sample CSV walked through, brief silence, laughter over mis-typed kernel name]
[40:01] Marcus Li: Wrapping up my side — we\'ll share the compatibility matrix CSV and the bench template. Also I\'ll include a short README for running benches in air-gapped mode.
[40:12] Jamie Ortega: Commercial recap: we\'ll propose a pilot for Oct-Nov focusing on two shortlisted models, include pilot credits, and a dev time estimate. We\'ll try to keep the SOW lightweight.
[40:25] Sara Patel: Sounds good. One ask — please make sure the SOW includes explicit measurements and acceptance criteria.
[40:31] Jamie Ortega: Absolutely.
[40:33] Evan Ross: Do you have any reference customers who did similar pilot?
[40:37] Jamie Ortega: We can share anonymized case studies — a fintech customer reduced token cost by ~40% via quant+cache and met latency targets with a mixed routing policy. We\'ll attach that.
[40:49] Lucas Meyer: Ok next steps — we\'ll assemble the prompt set and a short list of models we care about. Expect docs from us by Monday.
[40:58] Jamie Ortega: Great. To recap: Marcus to share matrix + bench template; Jamie to send pilot SOW and pricing; Priya to include private deployment checklist; Peregrine to share prompts and networking constraints.
[41:12] Nina Ortiz: And I\'ll work with Lucas on the network bits and share firewall rules.
[41:17] Marcus Li: One last thing — I\'ll add a column in the matrix for \"kernel risk\" and a link to build instructions.
[41:24] Sara Patel: Thanks all. That answered most questions.
[41:28] Jamie Ortega: Awesome, we\'ll follow up with the links and the SOW. Thanks everyone.
[41:33] [meeting ends]
questions: How often are fit tags updated?
Can bench runs be run in our private cluster?
What's required for private KMS integration?
